title: Neurophysiology (PIO 305/307)
description: Sensory receptors and pain, spinal reflexes, motor control by the cortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum, the autonomic nervous system, and special senses.

topics.title: Sensory Receptors and Pain
topics.summary: Receptor types, adaptation, sensory coding, and physiology of pain and its modulation.

notes.b: Sensory receptors transduce stimuli into receptor (generator) potentials. Types: mechanoreceptors (Meissner's corpuscles — light touch; Pacinian corpuscles — vibration, rapidly adapting; Merkel discs — sustained pressure; Ruffini endings — stretch; muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs — proprioception), thermoreceptors, nociceptors (free nerve endings), chemoreceptors and photoreceptors. Müller's law of specific nerve energies: each sensory pathway gives one modality regardless of how it is stimulated. Intensity is coded by frequency of action potentials and recruitment of receptors. Phasic (rapidly adapting) receptors signal change; tonic (slowly adapting) receptors signal sustained stimuli.

Nociceptors are free nerve endings. Fast, sharp, well-localised pain travels in myelinated Aδ fibres (neospinothalamic tract); slow, dull, burning, poorly localised pain travels in unmyelinated C fibres (paleospinothalamic tract). The gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) proposes that activity in large Aβ touch fibres inhibits pain transmission in the dorsal horn substantia gelatinosa — why rubbing an injury helps and TENS works. Descending inhibition from the periaqueductal grey and raphe nuclei uses endogenous opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) and serotonin. Referred pain is felt at a site distant from its origin because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal segment (e.g. cardiac pain to the left arm; diaphragmatic irritation to the shoulder tip, C3–C5).
k: Aδ: fast sharp pain; C: slow dull pain
Gate control theory: Aβ fibres close the gate

topics.title: Spinal Reflexes and Muscle Tone
topics.summary: The reflex arc, stretch reflex, muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and withdrawal reflexes.

notes.b: The stretch (myotatic) reflex is monosynaptic: stretching a muscle stretches muscle spindles (intrafusal fibres), whose Ia afferents synapse directly on α motor neurons supplying the same muscle, causing contraction (e.g. knee jerk, L3–L4). Reciprocal inhibition relaxes the antagonist via an inhibitory interneuron. γ motor neurons adjust spindle sensitivity (fusimotor control), which sets muscle tone. Golgi tendon organs, in series with the muscle, sense tension and via Ib afferents inhibit the contracting muscle (inverse stretch reflex/autogenic inhibition), protecting against excessive force.
k: γ motor neurons set spindle sensitivity
Golgi tendon organ: tension, Ib, autogenic inhibition

notes.b: Deep tendon reflex root values: biceps C5–C6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, knee L3–L4, ankle S1. The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is polysynaptic: a painful stimulus causes flexion of the limb, with the crossed extensor reflex extending the opposite limb to support body weight. After spinal cord transection there is initial spinal shock (areflexia, flaccidity), followed by hyperreflexia and spasticity below the lesion. The Babinski sign (extensor plantar) indicates an upper motor neuron lesion (normal in infants under about 1 year).
k: Biceps C5–6; triceps C7; knee L3–4; ankle S1

topics.title: Motor Control: Cortex, Basal Ganglia and Cerebellum
topics.summary: Motor pathways, the basal ganglia circuits, Parkinson's disease and cerebellar function.

notes.b: Voluntary movement is initiated by the primary motor cortex, premotor and supplementary motor areas, with the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract carrying commands. The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra) modulate movement through the direct pathway (facilitates movement) and indirect pathway (inhibits unwanted movement). Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway (D1) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D2). Parkinson's disease results from loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, causing bradykinesia, resting ('pill-rolling') tremor, cogwheel rigidity and postural instability; treated with levodopa plus carbidopa. Huntington disease (loss of striatal GABA neurons) causes chorea; lesions of the subthalamic nucleus cause hemiballismus.
k: Parkinson's: loss of substantia nigra dopamine neurons

notes.b: The cerebellum compares intended movement with actual movement (from proprioceptive input) and corrects errors, ensuring smooth, coordinated, accurate movements, balance and motor learning. Its only output is from Purkinje cells, which are inhibitory (GABA), to the deep cerebellar nuclei. The vestibulocerebellum controls balance and eye movements; the spinocerebellum controls posture and limb movement; the cerebrocerebellum plans skilled movements. Lesions produce intention tremor, dysmetria, ataxia, dysdiadochokinesia and nystagmus on the same side.
k: Lesions cause ipsilateral intention tremor and ataxia

topics.title: The Autonomic Nervous System
topics.summary: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, neurotransmitters, receptors and effects.

notes.b: The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions via a two-neuron chain (preganglionic and postganglionic). Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1–L2) with short preganglionic fibres to the paravertebral chain; parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4) with long preganglionic fibres to ganglia near or in target organs. All preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh on muscarinic receptors; most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline on adrenergic receptors — except sweat glands (sympathetic cholinergic). The adrenal medulla acts as a modified sympathetic ganglion releasing mainly adrenaline.
k: Parasympathetic: craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X, S2–4)

notes.b: α1 receptors: vasoconstriction, pupil dilation (radial muscle), bladder sphincter contraction. α2: presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release. β1: increased heart rate and contractility, renin release. β2: bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis. Muscarinic M2: slows the heart; M3: bronchoconstriction, glandular secretion, bladder detrusor contraction, pupil constriction. Sympathetic ('fight or flight') effects: tachycardia, bronchodilation, mydriasis, reduced gut motility, glycogenolysis. Parasympathetic ('rest and digest'): bradycardia, miosis, increased secretions and gut motility, micturition.

topics.title: Special Senses: Vision and Hearing
topics.summary: Optics and refraction errors, photoreceptors, the pupillary reflex, and the physiology of hearing and balance.

notes.b: Light is refracted mainly by the cornea (about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power) and fine-tuned by the lens. Accommodation for near vision involves ciliary muscle contraction (parasympathetic via CN III), making the lens rounder, with pupil constriction and convergence. Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation. Myopia (long eyeball) is corrected with concave lenses; hypermetropia with convex lenses; astigmatism with cylindrical lenses. Rods (rhodopsin, vitamin A) mediate dim-light, black-and-white vision and are absent from the fovea; cones mediate colour and acuity and are concentrated in the fovea. Phototransduction: light converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, closing Na+ channels and hyperpolarising photoreceptors.
k: Rods: dim light, vitamin A; cones: colour, fovea

notes.b: Sound waves vibrate the tympanic membrane; the ossicles amplify pressure (about 20-fold) into the oval window. In the cochlea, travelling waves along the basilar membrane stimulate hair cells in the organ of Corti: high frequencies are detected at the base, low frequencies at the apex. Endolymph (high K+) bathes hair cells. Conductive hearing loss (outer/middle ear: wax, otitis media, otosclerosis) versus sensorineural loss (cochlea or nerve: noise, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs like gentamicin) is distinguished with the Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests (512 Hz). Semicircular canals detect angular acceleration; the utricle and saccule (otoliths) detect linear acceleration and head position.
k: Base of cochlea: high frequency; apex: low
Rinne and Weber tests distinguish conductive vs sensorineural
